title: Squares and Cubes — Class 8 (NCERT / RL Public School Complete 34 Textbook Exercises)

questions.q: Which of the following numbers cannot be a perfect square based solely on its units digit? \(2032\), \(2048\), \(1027\), \(1089\)
questions.m: Students often test only the first candidate number or fail to recall that ending in 2, 3, 7, or 8 rules out a perfect square.

opts.m: Checked only the first ending digit while failing to recognize that integers ending in 7 or 8 cannot form squares.
Overlooked the ending digits 2 and 8, which can never terminate an integer square.
Assumed that ending in 9 disqualifies an integer, whereas 33 multiplied by 33 terminates in 9.

hints.h1: Recall the set of possible units digits for any square integer: 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9.
hints.h2: Any integer ending in 2, 3, 7, or 8 can immediately be ruled out as an integer square.
hints.h3: Inspect the final digit of each listed number against the disqualified list 2, 3, 7, 8.
hints.h4: Separate the values terminating in 2, 8, or 7 from values that could potentially be square.

questions.q: Which of the following expressions have the digit \(4\) in their units place? \(64^2, 108^2, 292^2, 36^2\)
questions.m: Conflating bases ending in 4 or 6 with bases ending in 2 or 8 when determining the units digit of squares.

opts.m: Confused bases ending in 4 or 6 (whose squares terminate in 6) with squares terminating in 4.
Assumed that a base ending in 4 generates a square ending in 4 rather than 6.
Assumed every even base generates a square terminating in identical units digits.

hints.h1: Observe the units digit of each base: 4, 8, 2, and 6.
hints.h2: Squaring a base ending in 2 or 8 always results in a units digit of 4.
hints.h3: Calculate only the square of each base's units digit: 4 times 4, 8 times 8, 2 times 2, 6 times 6.
hints.h4: Select the expressions whose base units digits square to a value terminating in 4.

questions.q: Find the length of the side of a square park whose area is \(441\text{ m}^2\).
questions.m: Dividing the area by two instead of extracting the principal square root.

opts.m: Divided the area value by two rather than extracting the square root.
Selected an integer whose square terminates in 1 but has total area below 400.
Chose a decade root that exceeds 900 when multiplied by itself.

hints.h1: Recall that the area of a square is calculated by side length multiplied by side length.
hints.h2: The side length corresponds to the principal square root of the given area.
hints.h3: Bracket between friendly squares: 20 squared denotes 400 and 30 squared denotes 900.
hints.h4: Find the integer between 20 and 30 whose units digit squares to 1.

questions.q: Find the cube roots of \(27000\) and \(10648\).
questions.m: Dividing numbers or trailing zero counts by two instead of three when evaluating cube roots.

opts.m: Divided trailing zeros by two rather than dividing the zero count by three for cube roots.
Divided the numerical values by three rather than extracting cubic factor triplets.
Underestimated the cube root of the five-digit integer into decade ten.

hints.h1: Decompose 27000 into 27 multiplied by 1000.
hints.h2: For 10648, inspect the units digit 8 to determine the units digit of its cube root.
hints.h3: Recall that cubing multiplies trailing zero counts by 3, so root extraction divides zero counts by 3.
hints.h4: Extract the cube roots of 27 and 1000 separately, and bracket 10648 between 20 cubed and 30 cubed.

questions.q: State whether the statement is True or False: 'The cube of any odd natural number is even.'
questions.m: Assuming that repeated multiplication of odd factors can change parity to even.

opts.m: Believed that repeated multiplication of odd factors can generate a factor of two.
Assumed parity behavior depends on the digit length of the base integer.
Confused prime factorisation properties with basic integer parity rules.

hints.h1: Test with a small odd integer such as 3.
hints.h2: Remember that the product of odd integers remains odd under multiplication.
hints.h3: Multiply 3 by 3, and then multiply that intermediate product by 3 again.
hints.h4: Notice that none of the three factors introduces divisibility by two.

questions.q: State whether the statement is True or False: 'There is no perfect cube that ends with the digit \(8\).'
questions.m: Applying square units digit limitations to cubic numbers.

opts.m: Applied square ending digit restrictions to cubes, forgetting cubes can terminate in any digit.
Overlooked two-digit counterexamples such as 12 cubed.
Confused base parity requirements with the impossibility of the ending digit.

hints.h1: Examine small natural cubes such as 1, 2, 3, 4.
hints.h2: Recall that 2 cubed produces a solid cube terminating in 8.
hints.h3: Test whether 12 cubed also terminates with the digit 8.
hints.h4: Any base integer ending in 2 produces a perfect cube terminating in 8.

questions.q: State whether the statement is True or False: 'The cube of a \(2\)-digit number may be a \(3\)-digit number.'
questions.m: Failing to check the lower bound: 10 cubed already occupies 4 digits.

opts.m: Assumed the cube of the smallest two-digit integer could have fewer than four digits.
Tested two-digit numbers without verifying the lower boundary cube.

opts.t: True for numbers ending in zero
opts.m: Did not check that 10 cubed already occupies four digit positions.

hints.h1: Identify the smallest possible two-digit natural number.
hints.h2: The smallest two-digit natural number is 10.
hints.h3: Compute the cube of 10 by evaluating 10 multiplied by 10 multiplied by 10.
hints.h4: Count the total digit positions in 1000 to determine the minimum digit count.

questions.q: State whether the statement is True or False: 'The cube of a \(2\)-digit number may have seven or more digits.'
questions.m: Overestimating the cubic expansion of two-digit numbers beyond the six-digit ceiling.

opts.m: Overestimated the growth rate of two-digit cubes beyond the upper limit.
Assumed integers in decade 90 can expand into seven digit positions.
Did not verify that 99 cubed remains strictly below one million.

hints.h1: Identify the largest possible two-digit natural number.
hints.h2: The largest two-digit natural number is 99, which is strictly below 100.
hints.h3: Compute the cube of 100: 100 cubed has seven digits.
hints.h4: Since 99 cubed is strictly less than 1000000, it can occupy at most six digit positions.

questions.q: Which of the following numbers can be definitively ruled out as a perfect square solely by inspecting its units digit?
questions.m: Assuming numbers ending in 4, 5, or 9 cannot be square, or failing to identify 7 as an impossible ending digit.

opts.m: Overlooked that integers terminating in 4 can be perfect squares, such as 32 squared.
Overlooked that integers terminating in 9 can be perfect squares, such as 33 squared.
Overlooked that integers terminating in 5 can be perfect squares, such as 45 squared.

hints.h1: Observe the units digit of each candidate number: 7, 4, 9, 5.
hints.h2: No square of any natural number can ever end in 2, 3, 7, or 8.
hints.h3: Locate the option terminating in one of the excluded digits: 2, 3, 7, or 8.
hints.h4: Identify the number ending in 7 as impossible for an integer square.

questions.q: If a natural number ends with \(3\) trailing zeros, how many trailing zeros will its square have?
questions.m: Adding zeros or squaring the zero count instead of multiplying the count by two.

opts.m: Assumed squaring preserves the identical number of trailing zeros without doubling.
Added two zeros rather than doubling the exponent count of ten.
Squared the count of zeros rather than multiplying the count by two.

hints.h1: Express the number as an integer multiplied by 10 cubed.
hints.h2: Under squaring, powers of ten multiply their exponent by two.
hints.h3: Test with 1000: evaluate 1000 multiplied by 1000.
hints.h4: Count the total number of zeros present in 1,000,000.

questions.q: What is the parity of the square of an odd natural number?
questions.m: Believing that squaring an odd number alters its parity to even.

opts.m: Believed that squaring any natural number converts the parity to divisible by two.
Assumed divisibility by three overrides basic parity rules.

opts.t: Can be either even or odd
opts.m: Assumed parity alternates unpredictably when squaring natural numbers.

hints.h1: Express an arbitrary odd integer in algebraic form: 2k + 1.
hints.h2: Expand the algebraic square: (2k + 1) squared.
hints.h3: Notice that 4k squared plus 4k is divisible by 2, leaving an extra remainder of 1.
hints.h4: Conclude that an odd integer multiplied by itself preserves uneven parity.

questions.q: What are all the integer solutions to the equation \(x^2 = 64\)?
questions.m: Omitting the negative root or mistaking quadratic roots for division.

opts.m: Overlooked that multiplying two negative values arrives at a positive product.
Disregarded the principal positive root when considering quadratic solutions.
Divided 64 by 4 rather than identifying integers whose square equals 64.

hints.h1: Recall that both positive and negative values can produce positive squares.
hints.h2: Test multiplying two identical positive integers and two identical negative integers to see both can reach 64.
hints.h3: A quadratic equation of the form x squared equals a positive value has two integer roots.
hints.h4: Account for both the positive principal root and its negative opposite.

questions.q: Given that \(125^2 = 15625\), what is the value of \(126^2\) using the consecutive squares property?
questions.m: Adding only 126 instead of adding 125 + 126 to step between consecutive squares.

opts.m: Added only the subsequent base rather than adding both consecutive bases n and n+1.
Doubled the next base without subtracting one in the consecutive odd increment.
Miscalculated the consecutive odd increment between the two squares.

hints.h1: Recall the algebraic identity: (n + 1) squared equals n squared plus 2n plus 1.
hints.h2: The difference between consecutive squares equals n plus (n + 1), which simplifies to 2n + 1.
hints.h3: Identify the base n as 125 and formulate the increment as the sum of 125 and its consecutive successor.
hints.h4: Add the two consecutive bases together to find the required increment, and attach it to 15625 to express 126 squared.

questions.q: Find the smallest natural number by which \(9408\) must be multiplied so that the product becomes a perfect square, and determine the square root of that product.
questions.m: Selecting already paired factors or miscalculating the combined square root.

opts.m: Selected an already paired prime factor rather than the lone unpaired factor.
Chose prime factor 7, which already appears with an even exponent.
Halved the root value by omitting one factor of two from the prime grouping.

hints.h1: Decompose 9408 into its prime factorisation.
hints.h2: Express 9408 in prime powers: 2 to the 6th power times 3 times 7 squared.
hints.h3: Identify which prime factor has an odd exponent and requires a partner.
hints.h4: Multiply by the unpaired prime and take one factor from each prime pair to determine the root.

questions.q: How many natural numbers lie strictly between \(16^2\) and \(17^2\)?
questions.m: Computing (n+1)^2 - n^2 = 2n+1 and forgetting to exclude the boundary square.

opts.m: Included one of the boundary squares by calculating the difference without subtracting one.
Subtracted two rather than one from the interval difference.
Provided the base integer n rather than applying the formula two times n.

hints.h1: Consider the interval of natural numbers strictly between the consecutive squares n squared and (n + 1) squared.
hints.h2: Subtracting the boundary squares and excluding endpoints yields (n + 1) squared minus n squared minus 1, which simplifies to 2n.
hints.h3: Identify the smaller base integer n in the given pair of squares 16 squared and 17 squared.
hints.h4: Apply the non-square count relation to that smaller base to find the exact number of intermediate natural numbers.

questions.q: A geometric vector array contains \(40\) distinct blocks of \(5 \times 5\) tiny squares. What is the total count of tiny squares and its prime factorisation?
questions.m: Multiplying 40 by 5 instead of 25, or miscounting prime powers in 1000.

opts.m: Multiplied 40 by 5 rather than multiplying 40 by 25.
Miscounted the prime exponent of two in the prime factorisation of 1000.
Assumed 40 blocks of 20 squares rather than 25 squares.

hints.h1: Calculate the number of tiny squares in one block of 5 by 5: evaluate 5 squared.
hints.h2: Multiply that block count by the total of 40 blocks to find the overall square count.
hints.h3: Express the resulting product as a power of 10.
hints.h4: Decompose the base 10 into its prime factors 2 and 5, applying the power of a product rule to find the prime factorisation.

questions.q: What is the smallest natural number by which \(1323\) must be multiplied so that the product becomes a perfect cube?
questions.m: Applying square grouping rules to cubes or trying to complete a factor that is already a triplet.

opts.m: Chose 3, which already appears as a complete triplet of prime factors.
Attempted to introduce additional powers of an already complete prime factor rather than completing the triplet for the incomplete prime factor.
Multiplied by the square of the incomplete prime rather than the single missing factor needed to complete a triplet.

hints.h1: Decompose 1323 into prime factors.
hints.h2: Observe that 1323 factors into a power of 3 and a power of an unpaired prime.
hints.h3: A perfect cube requires all prime exponents to be multiples of 3.
hints.h4: Determine the single prime factor needed to raise the squared prime factor to a cube.

questions.q: State whether the statement is True or False: 'A perfect cube always has an odd number of factors.'
questions.m: Overgeneralizing the odd factor property of squares to cubic numbers.

opts.m: Confused squares with cubes, assuming the odd factor count theorem applies to all powers.
Assumed base parity dictates factor count parity.
Believed odd cubes uniquely preserve odd divisor counts.

hints.h1: Test a counterexample such as 8, which corresponds to 2 cubed.
hints.h2: List all factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, and 8.
hints.h3: Count the total number of factors of 8.
hints.h4: Notice that 8 has four factors (an even count), disproving the claim.

questions.q: By grouping digits and inspecting units places, determine \(\sqrt[3]{12167}\) without full prime factorisation.
questions.m: Keeping the units digit 7 instead of finding its cubic ending complement 3, or overestimating the tens bracket.

opts.m: Retained the units digit 7 rather than taking the units complement for cube roots.
Overestimated the thousands group, forgetting 3 cubed exceeds 12.
Underestimated the tens group into decade ten.

hints.h1: Partition 12167 into two groups: 12 (thousands) and 167 (units group).
hints.h2: The units group ends in 7; recall which single digit cubed ends in 7.
hints.h3: Since 3 cubed terminates in 7, the units digit of the cube root corresponds to 3.
hints.h4: For the thousands group 12, bracket between 2 cubed (8) and 3 cubed (27).

questions.q: Why does a natural number have an odd number of factors if and only if it is a perfect square?
questions.ans: The factor pair \(a \times a = N\) has both partners equal, contributing only one unique factor.
questions.m: Confusing the parity of individual factor values with the count of divisors.

opts.t: The factor pair \(a \times a = N\) has both partners equal, contributing only one unique factor.
Every factor of a square number must be an odd number.
opts.m: Confused the count of factors with the parity of the individual factors.

opts.t: Squares have more prime factors than composite numbers.
opts.m: Believed squares inherently possess more prime factors than other composites.

opts.t: The prime exponents of a square are odd numbers.
opts.m: Inverted the prime exponent rule, forgetting exponents must be even for squares.

hints.h1: Consider how factors naturally pair up: a and b such that a times b equals N.
hints.h2: Observe what occurs when a number can be factored as a multiplied by itself.
hints.h3: In the pair where a equals b, the two partner factors denote the same integer.
hints.h4: Explain why this single self-partnered factor prevents the total factor count from remaining even.

questions.q: Given that \(35^2 = 1225\), find \(36^2\) using the consecutive odd numbers summation method.
questions.m: Adding 36 instead of the 36th odd number 71 to step to the next square.

opts.m: Added 36 rather than adding the 36th odd number.
Added 70 rather than adding the odd number 2(36) - 1.
Rounded to the nearest friendly decade rather than applying the odd summation step.

hints.h1: Recall that the square of any natural number n represents the sum of the first n consecutive odd natural numbers.
hints.h2: Because 35 squared is the sum of the first 35 odd numbers, obtaining 36 squared requires adding the 36th odd number to 1225.
hints.h3: Express the nth odd natural number using the general relation 2n - 1, setting n equal to 36.
hints.h4: Calculate the value of that 36th odd number and add it to 1225 to find the next square.

questions.q: How many non-square natural numbers lie strictly between \(12^2\) and \(13^2\)?
questions.m: Failing to exclude boundary squares or forgetting to double the smaller base.

opts.m: Computed the difference without subtracting one, including a boundary square.
Added one rather than subtracting one from the difference.
Stated the base value without multiplying by two.

hints.h1: Recall that the count of non-square natural numbers lying strictly between n squared and (n + 1) squared is given by 2n.
hints.h2: The count depends exclusively on doubling the smaller base of the two consecutive squares.
hints.h3: Identify the smaller base integer n from the given consecutive squares 12 squared and 13 squared.
hints.h4: Apply the doubling rule to that smaller base to determine the exact number of non-square natural numbers.

questions.q: What is the sum of the two consecutive triangular numbers \(T_4 = 10\) and \(T_5 = 15\)?

opts.m: Subtracted one from the sum of the two triangular numbers.
Multiplied the two triangular indices rather than summing the figurate values.

hints.h2: Notice that the sum of the (n-1)th and nth triangular numbers equals n squared.
hints.h3: Apply the property that the sum of consecutive triangular indices forms the square of the larger index.
hints.h4: Combine 10 and 15 to obtain the total square area.

questions.q: Using prime factorisation, determine whether \(1156\) is a perfect square, and find its square root if it is.
questions.m: Failing to recognize 289 as 17 squared or guessing roots based on units digits alone.

opts.m: Failed to recognize that 289 factors into 17 squared during prime division.
Chose 36 because its units digit squares to 6, without verifying prime factors.

hints.h1: Divide 1156 by 2 repeatedly: 1156 factors into 4 times 289.
hints.h2: Find the prime factors of 289: test prime candidates 13 and 17.
hints.h3: Observe that 289 equals 17 times 17, so 1156 equals 2 squared times 17 squared.
hints.h4: Group the factors into identical pairs: (2 times 17) squared.

questions.q: Estimate \(\sqrt{1936}\) by bracketing between decade squares and testing the midpoint \(45\).
questions.m: Choosing 46 despite 1936 being strictly less than 45 squared (2025).

opts.m: Selected 46 despite 1936 being strictly below 45 squared (2025).
Selected a root whose units digit squares to 4 rather than 6.

questions.q: Without adding the numbers one by one, find the sum of the \(10\) consecutive odd numbers: \(91 + 93 + 95 + 97 + 99 + 101 + 103 + 105 + 107 + 109\).
questions.m: Calculating 10 squared instead of 10 cubed, or misidentifying the odd partition block index.

questions.q: Find the smallest square number that is divisible by each of the numbers: \(4, 9,\) and \(10\).
questions.m: Stopping at the LCM without pairing odd prime factors, or over-multiplying beyond the minimum square.

opts.m: Stopped at the LCM rather than multiplying by the missing prime factor to form a square.
Multiplied by an unnecessary factor of 4 beyond the minimal square.
Doubled the LCM rather than multiplying by the unpaired prime factor required to complete square pairs.

hints.h2: Determine the prime factorisation of the LCM of 4, 9, and 10 by checking powers of 2, 3, and 5.
hints.h3: For a number to form a perfect square, every prime factor in its prime factorisation must have an even exponent.

questions.m: Misinterpreting the algebraic relationship between consecutive base products and the target sum base.

opts.m: Added 5 to 20 rather than adding 1 to 20 for the right-hand base.

questions.q: Which of the following expressions has the greatest numerical value? (i) \(67^3 - 66^3\), (ii) \(43^3 - 42^3\), (iii) \(67^2 - 66^2\), (iv) \(43^2 - 42^2\)
questions.m: Believing square differences can exceed cubic differences, or choosing a smaller base cube difference.

opts.m: Selected a cubic difference with a significantly smaller base.
Assumed square differences could exceed cubic differences of similar bases.
Selected the smallest expression among all four candidates.

hints.h1: Recall that (n+1) cubed minus n cubed equals 3n squared plus 3n plus 1.
hints.h2: Observe that cubic differences grow quadratically with the base n.
hints.h3: Square differences only grow linearly: (n+1) squared minus n squared equals 2n + 1.
hints.h4: Compare leading terms: 3 times 66 squared versus 3 times 42 squared.

questions.q: In the 'Square Pairs' challenge for numbers \(1\) to \(17\), adjacent pairs must sum to a square. Why must \(16\) and \(17\) be the two endpoints of the row?
questions.ans: In the square-sum connectivity graph, \(16\) and \(17\) each connect to only one other number (degree \(1\)).
questions.m: Assuming numerical magnitude rather than graph degree dictates Hamiltonian path endpoints.

opts.t: In the square-sum connectivity graph, \(16\) and \(17\) each connect to only one other number (degree \(1\)).
They are the two largest numbers in the given set.
opts.m: Assumed numerical size dictates endpoint placement in Hamiltonian paths.

opts.t: Their sum equals the largest possible perfect square.
opts.m: Overlooked that 16 plus 17 sums to 33, which does not form a square.

opts.t: Neither number can form a square sum with any even number.
opts.m: Disregarded that 17 pairs with 8 to form the square 25.

hints.h1: Count how many compatible partner numbers from 1 to 17 can add with 16 to form a perfect square.
hints.h2: Notice that 16 can only pair with 9 (16 + 9 = 25); no other integer in the set produces an allowed square sum.
hints.h3: Similarly test 17: it can only pair with 8 (17 + 8 = 25) to form an allowed square sum.
hints.h4: In a linear chain where every internal member must connect to two neighbors, any number possessing only a single valid partner cannot sit in the interior and must form an endpoint.

questions.q: In the 'Square Pairs' circle of numbers from \(1\) to \(32\), which of the following represents a valid adjacent pair whose sum is a perfect square?

hints.h3: Consider the sequence of consecutive perfect squares in this neighborhood: 6 squared (36), 7 squared (49), and 8 squared (64).
hints.h4: Determine which integer square falls within the interval from 48 to 52, and select the candidate pair that reaches that total.

questions.q: In Queen Ratnamanjuri's \(100\)-locker puzzle, which locker numbers remain OPEN after all \(100\) people have completed their turns?

questions.q: In Queen Ratnamanjuri's will, the secret vault passcode consists of the first five locker numbers that were touched exactly twice. What is the passcode?

questions.q: The taxicab number \(4104\) can be expressed as the sum of two cubes in two different ways: \(2^3 + 16^3\) and which other pair of cubes?

hints.h2: Because 16 cubed equals 4096, any other two cubes summing to 4104 must have positive integer bases strictly below 16.
hints.h3: Analyze which pairs of units digits for natural cubes sum to a units digit of 4, such as single digits ending in 9 and 5.
